phonemes.desc: Diphthong [eu̯] — a rounded glide from mid-close [e] to close [u], the standard Greek εὐ
Long open-mid back [ɔː] with acute and length mark; omega is a long o, not the modern English 'oh'
Voiceless bilabial stop [p] plus long close-mid front [ɛː], the Greek eta ē

pronunciation.approximation: 'ehv-ROH-pay' — begin with a quick 'eh-oo' glide, hold the 'roh' long, and finish with a stretched 'pay'.

pronunciation.note: Eurṓpē is a full Tier-1 Greek restoration: both the omega (length + stress) and the eta are long vowels, and the acute marks the pitch peak. The traditional 'wide-faced' etymology is Greek folk-etymology; the true pre-Greek origin — Greek or Semitic — remains uncertain.

domains.title: Personified Continent of Europe
domains.subtitle: The Tyrian Princess Who Named a Continent
domains.lead: Eurṓpē begins as a Phoenician princess gathering flowers on the Tyrian shore and ends as the name of a continent. Zeus, in the form of a white bull, carries her across the sea to Crete, where her sons — Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon — found the dynasties and afterlife judges of Greek imagination. Her myth is the charter of the West named for an Eastern girl: geography won in a single crossing.

cards.name: Bull from the Sea
cards.desc: Zeus took the form of a white bull and carried the Phoenician princess Eurṓpē across the sea to Crete.

cards.name: Continent Eponym
cards.desc: The land that received her took her name, making Europe a mythic body as well as a geographical space.

cards.name: Mother of Minos
cards.desc: Eurṓpē bore Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon, founding the Cretan dynasty and a judge of the dead.

cards.name: Western Horizon
cards.desc: Europe lay where the sun set; its name may echo a Semitic word for 'west', the realm of the setting sun.

mythology.lead: Eurṓpē is a myth of crossing: a Tyrian princess carried west on a god's back, whose name outgrew her story to label a continent. The sources delight in her — Moschus makes her the heroine of a little epic, Herodotus doubts her etymology, and Homer gives her a different father than Hesiod does. What survives every correction is the current she rides: from East to West, forever.

myths.title: Two Lands Quarrel over a Girl
myths.text: In Moschus' little epic Europa (2nd century BCE) the story opens inside a dream. The Tyrian princess sleeps, and two women struggle over her body: one in foreign dress, one Greek-speaking — Asia and Europe, fighting for the girl (Moschus, Europa 1–45). Europa wakes to gather flowers on the shore with her companions, and among the herds a great white bull stands, gentle as a pet, its breath sweet with crocus. The dream has already told us what the bull is: geography itself, come to carry her west. Ovid retells the omen (Metamorphoses 2.836–875) and gives the scene its permanent tension — a child playing on a god. The myth's first move is its most honest one: before any abduction happens, Europa already belongs to a quarrel between continents. A name on every modern map began as a dispute over one Phoenician girl.

myths.title: Carried Across the Sea
myths.text: Europa climbed onto the bull's back among the flowers, and the beast plunged into the sea. Moschus (Europa 46–165) makes the crossing gorgeous and terrifying: her veil streams, the Nereids rise and dance, Poseidon leads his train beneath the waves, and still she clutches one horn, her free arm lifted to the vanishing shore. Landfall came in Crete, in a grove of Gortyn, where the bull became Zeus and the marriage was divine. Her father Agenor sent her brothers Kadmos, Kilix, and Phoenix to find her or never return (Apollodorus, Library 3.1.1): the search failed, and each brother founded a land instead — Kilikia from Kilix, Phoenicia's royal line from Phoenix, and Thebes from Kadmos, who carried westward the alphabet itself. The myth quietly accounts for how the East reached Greece: Europa was carried, but her brothers walked, and everything they planted followed her.

myths.title: Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon
myths.text: Europa bore Zeus three sons — but the sources quarrel over the third. Homer knows Minos as her son and knows Sarpedon too, yet in the Iliad (6.198–199) Sarpedon is son of Zeus by Laodamia of Lycia; the Cretan tradition (Apollodorus, Library 3.1.1–2) makes him Europa's, and says she married Asterius, king of Crete, who adopted the boys. The middle son, Rhadamanthys, is the one Greek conscience loved: he ruled so justly that Plato stations him, with Minos and Aiakos, as a judge of the dead (Apology 41a; Gorgias 523e–524a). Apollodorus adds Europa's dowry-chest of wonders — Talos the bronze guardian, the dog Laelaps that never missed, the spear that never failed (3.2.1). One abduction thus produces the labyrinth's king, an afterlife judiciary, and a mythic arsenal. Whatever the genealogists dispute, the pattern holds: law itself, in the Greek imagination, descends from the carried girl.

myths.title: The Continent Takes Her Name
myths.text: How did a Phoenician princess become a continent? Herodotus reports the Greeks' own answer — and his doubts: the lands were named for women, Asia for a wife of Prometheus, Libya for a nymph, and Europe 'after the Tyrian Europa', though whether the earth is really divided so 'no man knows' (Herodotus 4.45). Behind the etymology stands an older, different genealogy: Hesiod's Theogony (357) lists Europa among the Oceanids, daughters of Ocean, and Homer (Iliad 14.321–322) calls her daughter of Phoenix. The land-name itself appears among the early geographers (Hecataeus, FGrHist 1) before any heroine; many philologists hear a Semitic word behind it — ʿereb, 'west, sunset', the direction from which evening comes. Europe, in the most economical reading, was the West before it was a girl. But myth out-argues philology: for two and a half millennia the West has preferred to be named for someone carried toward it.

lore.syncretism: Rome took the myth without building her a cult — no temple of Europa stood in the city; she persisted as an image. Roman floor mosaics across the empire, from North Africa to Syria, spread the bull-riding princess through the provinces, and Ovid's retelling made her a set piece of school recitation. The Middle Ages allegorized her: in the Ovide moralisé tradition the bull became Christ, carrying the soul-Europa across the sea of the world to salvation. The modern age re-materialized her: when Galileo's moons needed names, Simon Marius called the second one Europa (1614); Titian's Rape of Europa (c. 1562) hangs in Boston as the myth's supreme painting; and since 2013 her portrait watermarks every banknote of the euro's 'Europa series'. A Phoenician girl abducted by a god now certifies the currency of a continent she never saw — the strangest promotion in mythology.
lore.culturalLegacy: Europa is the only continent whose name carries a story, and the story is an abduction — the West named for a girl carried west. Greek 2-euro coins strike her riding the bull; the European Central Bank chose her face as the hologram of its banknotes; an ocean moon of Jupiter bears her name over a sea of ice. In scholarship her myth became a textbook of method: Herodotus doubting the etymology, Hesiod giving a different father, Homer a different son for Sarpedon — a case study in how stories accrete around names. Every map of Europe is, in the end, a retelling of Moschus' dream: two lands quarrelling over a girl, and the girl becoming the prize.
lore.extendedMeditation:
What does it mean that a civilization named itself after an abducted teenager? Europa's myth is the myth of eponymy itself — the moment a story hardens into a label. The Greeks needed the West to have a face, and chose an Eastern one: Europe is named for an import, carried across the sea it now borders.

That is a more honest foundation than most. Continents are conventions, lines argued over by geographers and empires; Europa's story admits as much while insisting the convention still needs a soul. Every time the name is spoken — in councils, on coins, on a moon of Jupiter — the old dream flickers: two lands quarrelling over one girl, and the girl, who had no say in any of it, outlasting both the quarrel and the lands.
lore.archaeology: Europa's oldest described image in art is lost but recorded: the cedar chest of Cypselus at Olympia (before 580 BCE) showed her riding the bull, and Pausanias (5.19.1) noted the scene among its earliest panels. Coins of Gortyn in Crete — the city of her landing — carry the motif from archaic times onward: the girl in the branches of the sacred plane tree, the bull beside her. That tree had a long afterlife: travellers were shown the plane of Gortyn under which Zeus lay with Europa well into late antiquity (Procopius, Buildings 4). Roman floor mosaics from North Africa to the Levant repeat the sea-crossing, and fragments from Antioch and Apamea keep her sidesaddle on the bull across the whole empire.
